Germany.title: Germany
gridConnectionProcedure: Renewable electricity installations have a priority connection right under Section 8 EEG. Section 8a permits agreed flexible connection limits. The applicable connection point is determined under the statutory technical and economic criteria. The NAV governs low-voltage electricity consumption connections; Section 1 excludes connections of renewable generation installations. Applicable technical connection rules, including VDE-AR-N 4105 for low-voltage generation, and the DSO’s requirements must also be observed.
strategiesvolatility: Under the Section 14a EnWG framework, DSOs may temporarily limit grid imports by eligible controllable devices to address congestion. The basic minimum remaining power is 4.2 kW; this is not the maximum amount of a reduction. Different calculation rules apply to larger heat pumps and air-conditioning systems and to control through an energy management system.

The framework generally covers qualifying devices with a connection capacity above 4.2 kW commissioned from 1 January 2024 on low-voltage networks: private EV chargers, heat pumps, air-conditioning systems and storage when importing electricity. Participants receive reduced network charges.
Since 1 April 2025, eligible customers can combine the time-variable network tariff under Module 3 with Module 1, subject to the required metering arrangements.
Grid-supporting inverter behaviour under VDE-AR-N 4105 helps to stabilise voltage in low-voltage networks with high photovoltaic penetration.
regulatoryFramework: Energy Industry Act: EnWG, especially Section 14a.
Renewable Energy Sources Act: EEG, especially Sections 8 ff.
Low Voltage Connection Ordinance: NAV.
Metering Point Operation Act: MsbG.
Technical rules: VDE-AR-N 4100 and VDE-AR-N 4105.
responsibleInstitutions: Bundesnetzagentur: national regulatory authority.
Local distribution system operators: e.g. Westnetz, Bayernwerk, Netze BW, E.DIS.
VDE FNN: technical connection rules.
implementationExamples: From 2024 onwards, new controllable devices cannot generally be refused connection merely because of potential congestion; instead, the DSO may temporarily limit consumption during critical grid situations.
EV chargers or heat pumps may be reduced to a lower operating level rather than disconnected completely.
Reduced network charges create a financial incentive for consumers to provide flexibility.

AgNes is an ongoing electricity network tariff reform. The Bundesnetzagentur’s 2026 timetable envisages a framework decision in late 2026 and implementation from 2029; proposed design elements must not be treated as final rules as of 28 October 2026.
newconsumersandflexibleloads: Qualifying private EV chargers, heat pumps, storage importing electricity and air-conditioning systems are covered by the Section 14a framework, subject to its capacity, commissioning and connection criteria.

The Bundesnetzagentur’s MiSpeL determination of October 2026 provides accounting rules for mixed-use storage, including bidirectional charging, to preserve support for eligible renewable exports while allowing grid charging.
MiSpeL provides an allocation option (Abgrenzungsoption) and a simplified option (Pauschaloption) for eligible small PV configurations up to 30 kWp.

sources.name: Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWE)

latestUpdates: MiSpeL has a transition period until September 2027. Earlier application requires the relevant network and metering operators’ agreement; the simplified option also depends on European Commission state-aid approval.

The EEG reform for the period after 2026 remained a legislative process at the review date. The expiry of a state-aid approval period must not be confused with the automatic termination of existing installations’ EEG remuneration entitlements.

Network Tariff Reform (AgNes): The Federal Network Agency published a draft reform of electricity network charges in 2026. Final provisions and implementation dates remain subject to regulatory decisions.

comparison.gridOperators: TSOs: 50Hertz, Amprion, TenneT, TransnetBW; DSOs: local network operators.
comparison.connectionProcedure: Application to the DSO → technical assessment → applicable connection rules → metering and control arrangements → commissioning.
comparison.legalBasis: EnWG, EEG, NAV, MsbG, §14a EnWG, VDE-AR-N 4105.
comparison.implementationExample: Controllable EV chargers, heat pumps and batteries may be temporarily limited during grid congestion in exchange for reduced grid fees.

Austria.title: Austria
Austria.gridConnectionProcedure: Renewable installations apply to the responsible network operator and must meet applicable technical connection requirements. The ElWG introduces connection-charge reforms in stages. Annex V includes EUR 13/kW for the 0–20 kW grid-effective capacity band, subject to the applicable commencement and charging provisions. Section 96 provides a separate connection exemption for qualifying PV installations up to 15 kW using an existing consumption connection. This must not be confused with the 20 kW exemption from the annual infrastructure contribution under Section 75a.
strategiesvolatility: Austria combines hydropower, storage and demand-side flexibility.
Hydropower, pumped storage, batteries and demand-side management provide flexibility; smart meters and grid monitoring support their coordination.
Smart Grids Austria and APG particularly emphasize the importance of intelligent grids for integrating renewable energy.

Since 1 April 2026, the SNAP summer tariff reduces the eligible volumetric network charge by 20% between 10:00 and 16:00 from April to September, subject to the applicable metering and tariff conditions.
At the distribution network level, intelligent local substations, grid monitoring, and controllable consumers are important technical solutions.
regulatoryFramework: Key legal foundations include the Renewable Expansion Act (EAG).
The Electricity Industry Act 2025 (Elektrizitätswirtschaftsgesetz, ElWG) replaces the ElWOG 2010 through staged commencement and repeal provisions in Section 188.
EU Directive 2018/2001 on renewable energy.
EU Directive 2019/944 on the internal electricity market.
The EAG provides renewable support and rules for renewable energy communities; citizen energy communities have a separate electricity-market-law basis, now within the ElWG framework.
ElWG regulates market organisation, grid operation, market roles, and security of supply.
responsibleInstitutions: E-Control is the national regulatory authority supervising the electricity and gas markets.
Federal Ministry of Economy, Energy and Tourism (BMWET) is responsible for energy policy.
Austrian Power Grid (APG) is Austria’s main transmission system operator and control-area manager.
Distribution system operators are responsible for local grid connections.
The Austrian Coordination Office for Energy Communities supports practical implementation.
implementationExamples: E-Control’s 2025 monitoring report records a smart-meter rollout of 96.9% as at 31 December 2024.
Energy communities play a particularly important role in Austria.

Renewable energy communities and citizen energy communities allow eligible participants to share generation and consumption under their respective legal frameworks; membership, geographical and operational conditions differ.

Local energy sharing can increase self-consumption and enable community business models. Reductions in losses or congestion depend on the location and timing of generation and demand; they are not automatic outcomes.
newconsumersandflexibleloads: New consumers mainly include heat pumps, EV charging stations (wallboxes), battery storage systems, and prosumer households. These increase the local grid load but can also support the grid through intelligent control.
Heat pumps can use thermal storage, electric vehicles can shift charging times, and battery storage systems can reduce PV feed-in peaks.
As a result, flexibility in distribution grids has become a key component of Austria’s energy transition.

Section 68 ElWG provides for peer-to-peer electricity arrangements within the active-customer framework, with the relevant provisions effective from 1 October 2026 and subject to their contractual and market conditions.
Section 188 brings specified active-customer and sharing provisions into effect on 1 October 2026; this date must not be attributed indiscriminately to every right in Section 65 ElWG.

sources.name: Federal Ministry of Economy, Energy and Tourism (BMWET)
RIS: Renewable Expansion Act, English translation of 2021 (historical; check amendments)
RIS: Electricity Industry Act 2025 (ElWG), BGBl. I 91/2025

latestUpdates: From 1 January 2027, Section 75a ElWG provides for a generation infrastructure contribution, subject to the implementing rate and statutory conditions. Installations with grid-effective capacity up to and including 20 kW are exempt.
From 1 January 2027, Section 101 ElWG permits qualifying wind-generation peak curtailment, subject to statutory exceptions and limits of 1% of the reference annual energy and 15% of capacity.
Transition from ElWOG 2010: Remaining provisions on network charges under §§51–58a ElWOG 2010 expire on 31 December 2026 as the new ElWG framework takes effect.

comparison.gridOperators: Austrian Power Grid (APG); regional DSOs (e.g. Netz NÖ, Netz OÖ, Wiener Netze).
comparison.connectionProcedure: Connection request → capacity assessment → technical approval → applicable TOR requirements → commissioning. E-Control reported 96.9% smart-meter deployment as at 31 December 2024.
comparison.legalBasis: Elektrizitätswirtschaftsgesetz (ElWG), Erneuerbaren-Ausbau-Gesetz (EAG), and applicable TOR technical rules.
comparison.implementationExample: Smart-grid approaches can coordinate PV, heat pumps and EV charging using monitoring and flexibility management; the original text does not identify a specific project for verification.

Turkey.title: Turkey
gridConnectionProcedure: Applications for unlicensed generation are submitted to the relevant distribution or organised industrial zone network operator. For applicable solar and wind projects, the EİGM roadmap specifies a 30-day technical evaluation stage; this is not a deadline for the entire connection process. TEİAŞ published procedures for jointly financed transmission investments in February 2026.
strategiesvolatility: Permitted mechanical and electrical capacity must be checked against the applicable unlicensed-generation category and project approval date. A universal two-to-one ratio has not been verified for all installations.

Verification note: the blanket description of monthly netting is outdated. Reports on the 2026 reform describe hourly netting for relevant unlicensed installations; the applicable exceptions and transition rules require confirmation against the official EPDK text.
TEİAŞ publishes technical criteria and testing requirements for storage participation in ancillary services. The applicable version must be checked for the particular service and connection.
regulatoryFramework: The central regulatory framework is the Regulation on Unlicensed Electricity Generation (Lisanssız Elektrik Üretimi).
Storage installations are subject to applicable connection, compatibility and operational requirements. TEİAŞ technical documents must be distinguished from EPDK licensing and market regulations.
responsibleInstitutions: The regulatory authority is the EPDK.
The transmission grid is centrally operated by TEİAŞ.
Regional distribution companies and organised industrial zone network operators handle relevant distribution connections; the operator responsible for the site must be identified.
implementationExamples: At DC fast-charging stations, some charging network operators may terminate the charging service once the battery reaches 85% state of charge, provided that users are informed in advance. This is intended to improve the efficient use of fast-charging infrastructure.
newconsumersandflexibleloads: Household battery installations must comply with the applicable storage, connection, metering and safety rules; permission cannot be inferred solely from the voluntary nature of installation.

Storage remuneration depends on the generation and storage category, metering and applicable settlement rules. The assertion that every storage export is unpaid and transferred to a state fund is not established; YEKDEM is a renewable support mechanism, not a general state purchaser of all storage exports.

Charging network operators require an EPDK licence. Individual charging-station operators may operate under a certificate issued by a licensed network operator; private charging is not automatically subject to the same licensing requirement.
TEİAŞ published updated announcements and participation arrangements for demand-side services, supporting the involvement of flexible electricity consumers in system operation.

sources.name: Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources; EİGM is its Directorate General of Energy Affairs
EPDK – Erklärung Nr. 1 zur lizenzfreien Erzeugung [document contents not fully accessible]

latestUpdates: Verification note: the claimed universal commencement of ancillary-service amendments on 1 January 2027 and infrastructure deadline of 31 December 2026 were not sufficiently verified in the official legal text. They are not presented as confirmed obligations.
TEİAŞ published the 2027 capacity-mechanism application announcement in August 2026 and a subsequent application-assessment announcement in October 2026.

comparison.gridOperators: TEİAŞ; regional distribution companies (e.g. Başkent EDAŞ, AYEDAŞ, Toroslar EDAŞ).
comparison.connectionProcedure: Connection application → capacity evaluation → technical compliance → connection agreement → commissioning.
comparison.legalBasis: Electricity Market Law No. 6446, connection and system-use rules, and the Regulation on Unlicensed Electricity Generation.
comparison.implementationExample: Unlicensed-generation procedures provide a framework for eligible rooftop PV and other qualifying projects, subject to capacity and connection requirements.

Portugal.title: Portugal
gridConnectionProcedure: Decree-Law 15/2022 governs Portugal’s electricity system, as amended, including by Decree-Law 130/2026 of 29 June 2026. Law 29/2026 simplifies applicable renewable self-consumption procedures; licence deadlines and tacit approval apply only where their statutory conditions are met. Network connection also requires the relevant operator’s technical assessment. Decree-Law 100/2026 addresses dynamic management of already allocated connection capacity.
strategiesvolatility: Portugal strongly relies on self-consumption, collective self-consumption and renewable energy communities to balance generation and demand closer to the point of use.
The self-consumption regulation defines 15-minute energy balancing intervals, which is relevant for allocating consumption and injection in decentralised systems.
Smart grid services and digital metering are used to improve data availability, transparency and network operation.
regulatoryFramework: Decree-Law 100/2026 of 22 May 2026 establishes a complementary regime for the dynamic management of allocated connection capacity to the public electricity network (RESP).

Law 29/2026 of 23 June 2026 includes 90-day deadlines for the production and operating licences covered by its provisions, with tacit approval subject to statutory conditions. This does not mean every small self-consumption installation requires both licences.
Decree-Law 15/2022, as amended, is the principal legal framework for the national electricity system.
Decree-Law 130/2026 of 29 June 2026 amends Decree-Law 15/2022 in relation to renewable energy and electricity-market requirements.
Regulamento n.º 827/2023, Commercial Relations Regulations for the Electricity and Gas Sectors.
Self-consumption: Regulation 815/2023, as amended, including by Regulation 8/2026; the ERSE approval document is also identified internally as Regulation 2/2023.
Regulation 8/2026 amends several ERSE regulations, including the self-consumption framework.
ERSE Regulation No. 1218/2025 establishes the electricity tariff framework, with regulatory parameters covering 2026–2029.
ERSE rules on smart grids, metering and electric mobility.
responsibleInstitutions: ERSE: national regulatory authority for energy services.
DGEG: Directorate-General for Energy and Geology, responsible for energy policy, strategic framework and legislation.
E-REDES is the main distribution system operator in mainland Portugal.
implementationExamples: Collective self-consumption allows several consumers to share locally produced renewable electricity.
Renewable energy communities can use UPAC generation and distribute benefits among members.
E-REDES provides operational information for production licensing and connection to the RESP.
newconsumersandflexibleloads: Relevant resources include self-consumption generation (UPAC), storage, EV charging and collective self-consumption arrangements. Generation and community arrangements are not themselves simply additional electricity loads.
Electric mobility is regulated through ERSE’s Electric Mobility Regulation, covering charging point operators, service providers, measurement, data provision and price supervision.
Law No. 29/2026 introduces CAER contracts, allowing property owners to grant renewable energy utilisation rights for self-consumption installations up to 1 MW (06/26).
latestUpdates: Revised mainland tariff periods are scheduled from 1 April 2027 for BTE, MT, AT and MAT customers, and progressively from July to December 2027 for BTN customers with two- or three-period tariffs.

Verification note: the asserted end-2027 availability of the regulated electricity tariff has not been sufficiently established here against the applicable extension legislation. Eligibility and the current transition timetable require separate confirmation.

comparison.regulatoryAuthority: ERSE is the energy regulator; DGEG is the administrative authority for energy and geology.
comparison.gridOperators: Mainland Portugal: REN for transmission; E-REDES as the main distribution operator. Island systems have separate arrangements.
comparison.connectionProcedure: Applicable registration or licensing → network assessment → connection arrangements → metering and settlement. ERSE’s 2025 smart-grid report is the relevant source for deployment statistics; the unverified 1 July 2025 snapshot is omitted.
comparison.legalBasis: Decree-Law 15/2022 as amended; self-consumption Regulation 815/2023 as amended; applicable ERSE tariff, metering and electric-mobility regulations.
comparison.implementationExample: Collective self-consumption (UPAC) and Renewable Energy Communities (CER) share locally generated renewable electricity.

France.title: France
gridConnectionProcedure: In Enedis areas, applications can be submitted online. A revised connection-cost schedule takes effect on 28 October 2026. Offer deadlines depend on the connection category and a complete application; six weeks is not a universal deadline. Required conformity documentation, including CONSUEL certification where applicable, must be obtained before commissioning. CONSUEL is a conformity-assessment organisation, not the energy regulator, and a Linky meter may already be installed.
strategiesvolatility: Time-of-use options such as heures pleines/heures creuses and EDF’s Tempo tariff provide different price signals. They are not a single nationally uniform load-control scheme.
Compatible controls can schedule appliances, such as water heaters, around tariff periods. A smart meter alone does not automatically control every thermal load in response to network utilisation.
The annual TURPE adjustment took effect on 1 August 2026 for the relevant transmission and distribution network tariffs.
regulatoryFramework: Eligible renewable installations may receive support through purchase obligations or other applicable schemes. Self-consumption with surplus export is one configuration; EDF is not the only possible obligated purchaser and eligibility depends on the scheme.
Collective Self-Consumption (Decree No. 2026-561).
The standard French self-consumption framework accounts for imports and surplus exports separately rather than using retail net metering.
responsibleInstitutions: The Commission de Régulation de l'Énergie (CRE) acts as the NRA.
RTE is the transmission system operator. Enedis is the main distribution operator in metropolitan France; local distribution companies and island arrangements also exist.
implementationExamples: Collective self-consumption allows eligible participants to allocate locally generated electricity through metering and settlement arrangements. The standard extended scheme uses a maximum distance of 2 km between the most distant participants, subject to exceptions; this is not a 2 km radius. Allocations use the applicable settlement intervals.
newconsumersandflexibleloads: Residential storage can increase self-consumption or provide flexibility. Its adoption and profitability depend on equipment costs, tariff arrangements and operating conditions; no causal claim about a minor national role is established here.
Bidirectional EV charging can provide flexibility where compatible vehicles, chargers, contracts and network arrangements are available. No claim of nationwide commercial availability is made.

PV support eligibility must be checked against the current tariff orders and tender rules for the relevant installation size and application date. A general entitlement for all installations up to 500 kW is not established by this review.
Decree 2026-561 of 26 June 2026 changes collective self-consumption allocation rules. Its provisions have different commencement dates; Article 1(1) applies from 1 July 2027 under Article 2.

sources.name: Enedis: preliminary network development planning document for 2027 and 2032
Légifrance – Arrêté du 21 novembre 2019, proximité géographique

latestUpdates: From 1 July 2027, additional provisions of Decree No. 2026-561 take effect, modifying electricity allocation arrangements within collective self-consumption projects.

Spain.title: Spain
Spain.gridConnectionProcedure: National and regional approval procedures, technical connection requirements, and grid capacity assessments shape the connection of renewable energy installations. Large PV and wind projects are often connected to Red Eléctrica's transmission network, while self-consumption systems and community PV projects are mainly connected to distribution grids. The key challenge is balancing very high solar generation peaks with regional demand, available grid capacity, and storage.
strategiesvolatility: Spain relies on grid expansion, energy storage, self-consumption, collective self-consumption, flexibility, and improved market integration of renewable energy.
PV self-consumption can reduce electricity fed into the public grid when generation and consumption coincide locally.
Batteries can absorb midday PV generation and discharge later. Flexible consumption can be shifted into periods of high PV output, rather than from midday into the evening.
regulatoryFramework: The main legal foundations are Royal Decree 244/2019 on self-consumption.
Royal Decree-Law 23/2020.
Additional national and EU provisions govern renewable energy communities and citizen energy communities; their legal definitions and requirements differ.
The EU Renewable Energy Directive and the EU Electricity Market Directive are also relevant.
Regulatory priorities focus on simplifying self-consumption, collective use, metering, billing, and grid access.
responsibleInstitutions: MITECO is the ministry responsible for ecological transition and energy policy.
IDAE supports programmes, advisory services, and implementation of self-consumption and energy communities.
CNMC is the national regulatory authority for competition and markets.
Red Eléctrica (REE) is the transmission system operator and system manager.
Regional authorities and distribution system operators play a key role in approval and grid connection processes.

The CNMC resolution of 31 July 2026 establishes four flexible demand access-permit types, effective from 1 September 2026. Eligibility depends on voltage level, capacity and control arrangements; these are not universal household connection options.
implementationExamples: Collective self-consumption and energy communities provide examples of shared renewable generation; this is an illustrative assessment, not a verified international best-practice ranking.
Possible lessons for Germany include shared PV arrangements, storage integration and billing design; transferability depends on German law and network conditions.

Clear procedures for metering, allocation and billing can facilitate collective self-consumption. The reviewed material does not establish regulatory simplification as a quantified causal success factor.
newconsumersandflexibleloads: New consumers in Spain primarily include electric vehicles, heat pumps in certain building segments, battery storage systems, prosumers, and commercial self-consumption systems.
Collective self-consumption is especially important: multiple consumers can jointly use a single generation facility, for example in apartment buildings, neighbourhoods, or municipal projects.
This transforms consumers into active market participants.
latestUpdates: Applications for flexible access-permit Types 0, 1 and 3 must become available within six months of 1 September 2026. This is a future implementation deadline, not evidence that all types were already available at the review date.
Type 2 flexible demand access permits must become available no later than 1 January 2028, subject to the framework’s eligibility and monitoring requirements.

Italy.title: Italy
Italy.gridConnectionProcedure: Renewable energy installations are connected through the responsible grid operators. Large installations are often connected to Terna's transmission network, while rooftop PV systems, prosumers, and battery storage systems are primarily connected to the distribution grid. The key challenge lies in the geographical distribution: renewable generation is often located where grid capacity is limited, whereas major consumption centres are situated in other regions. Terna addresses this development in its National Grid Development Plan, which outlines the expansion of the national transmission infrastructure and the integration of renewable energy.
strategiesvolatility: Italy places a strong emphasis on digitalisation.
Second-generation smart meters provide interval data and can support network-quality monitoring and consumer feedback. Available functions depend on the meter and communications system.
ARERA considers the further development of smart metering and flexibility services for distribution networks to be a strategic priority.
In addition, battery storage, demand response, aggregators, and grid expansion are important instruments for limiting volatility.
regulatoryFramework: Key legal foundations include Legislative Decree 199/2021 implementing the Renewable Energy Directive.
Legislative Decree 210/2021 implementing the EU Electricity Market Directive.

The framework also includes ARERA’s TICA connection rules, smart-metering and tariff decisions, and applicable technical standards, including CEI 0-21 for low-voltage and CEI 0-16 for medium-voltage connections.
Smart metering, consumer protection and flexibility services are governed by related regulatory and technical requirements.
responsibleInstitutions: ARERA is the national regulatory authority for energy, networks, and consumer protection.
Terna is the transmission system operator and system manager.
GSE is responsible for renewable energy support and settlement mechanisms.
MASE is the Ministry of the Environment and Energy Security.
Distribution system operators such as e-distribuzione and Areti implement smart metering and local grid connections in practice.
implementationExamples: Italy’s extensive smart-meter deployment is a relevant implementation example; this is not a quantified ranking of national best practices.
Possible lessons for Germany include using metering data to support network monitoring and flexibility, subject to suitable communications, control equipment and market rules.
Digital distribution-network monitoring can facilitate PV integration and flexible demand, alongside adequate network capacity, protection and operational arrangements.
newconsumersandflexibleloads: New electricity consumers mainly include electric vehicles, heat pumps, prosumer households, battery storage systems, and flexible commercial and industrial processes.

Italy's smart meter infrastructure represents a major advantage: electricity consumption and feed-in can be monitored in greater detail, enabling flexible tariffs, consumer feedback, grid monitoring, and, in the future, enhanced flexibility services.

sources.name: ARERA: Annual Report Summary 2024 (historical reporting period)
National Electricity Transmission Grid Development Plan (Terna)
IEA Policies: Approval of rollout of second-generation smart meters by DSOs

latestUpdates: ARERA’s TIDE dispatching framework has applied since 2025 and supports the participation of qualifying resources in system services. This review does not establish that there will be no important changes at the beginning of 2027.

comparison.connectionProcedure: Connection application → network study → applicable CEI standards → metering → commissioning.
comparison.legalBasis: Legislative Decree 199/2021, ARERA resolutions, CEI 0-21 (LV), CEI 0-16 (MV).
comparison.implementationExample: The ongoing deployment of second-generation meters includes e-distribuzione’s Open Meter programme; other DSOs use their own metering programmes.

Netherlands.title: Netherlands
gridConnectionProcedure: The Dutch electricity system is regulated through the Netcode Elektriciteit, which sets rules for network operation, grid connection and electricity transport. Due to severe grid congestion, grid connection is no longer only a technical procedure but increasingly a capacity allocation problem. In congested areas, new renewable generation, batteries, heat pumps, charging stations and industrial loads may face waiting lists or conditional connection arrangements.
strategiesvolatility: The Netherlands provides examples of congestion management and incentives for large users to adapt network use during constrained periods.
Congestion management rules allow system operators and large users to free up capacity for renewable projects, EV charging infrastructure, heat pumps and other electrified loads.
Flexible grid use, off-peak contracts and congestion steering contracts are increasingly used to make better use of existing capacity.
regulatoryFramework: Energiewet, largely effective from 1 January 2026, together with applicable implementing rules and transitional provisions.
Netcode Elektriciteit.
ACM code decisions on congestion management and flexible use of the grid.
responsibleInstitutions: ACM: Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets, national regulatory authority.
TenneT: transmission system operator.
Regional DSOs: Liander, Enexis, Stedin.
implementationExamples: ACM has approved measures that financially reward large users for reducing consumption during peak periods.

TenneT’s 2025 reporting identified potential to unlock up to 9 GW through off-peak access arrangements. This is potential use of existing network capacity, not proof that more than 9 GW of firm physical capacity has already been delivered.
Flexible access can make better use of existing networks and complement reinforcement; it does not eliminate the need for grid expansion.
newconsumersandflexibleloads: EV charging stations, heat pumps, electric boilers, battery systems, data centres and industrial electrification projects.
Unmanaged new demand can increase coincident peaks. Storage and controllable demand can also relieve congestion when operated at suitable times and locations.
latestUpdates: ACM adopted regulatory methodologies for 2027–2031 in February 2026. Separately, household PV net metering under the salderingsregeling is scheduled to end on 1 January 2027; exported electricity will instead be remunerated under the applicable rules.

Denmark.title: Denmark
gridConnectionProcedure: Applicants contact the network operator responsible for the proposed connection. DSOs handle distribution connections, while Energinet handles transmission connections and relevant system requirements. Applicable Danish technical rules and European network codes depend on the installation and voltage level.
strategiesvolatility: Denmark uses market-based flexibility, dynamic price signals and short-term electricity markets to integrate large shares of wind and solar power.
Energinet highlights that the need for flexibility increases with renewable energy expansion and that 15-minute trading supports better balancing of forecast errors and variable generation.
Danish regulators emphasise cost-reflective tariffs, transparency and non-discrimination when designing flexibility-oriented tariff structures.
regulatoryFramework: Danish Electricity Supply Act (Elforsyningsloven), consolidated as LBK 544 of 16 June 2026, with applicable subsequent amendments.
Danish Renewable Energy Act (Lov om fremme af vedvarende energi), including applicable amendments.
Applicable implementing orders and technical connection requirements must be identified for the installation type; the original text does not specify their numbers or versions.
Energinet technical rules and market rules.
responsibleInstitutions: Danish Utility Regulator: national regulatory authority.
Energinet: transmission system operator.
Distribution system operators include N1 and Radius Elnet.
implementationExamples: 15-minute intraday trading and balancing market reforms allow market participants to adjust production and consumption closer to real time.
Tariff reform and digitalisation are being used to activate demand-side flexibility.
newconsumersandflexibleloads: Electric vehicles, heat pumps, data centres, Power-to-X, electrolysers and industrial electrification are considered important future flexibility resources.
Denmark is especially relevant because demand-side flexibility is linked to wind power integration and sector coupling.

sources.name: Energinet – Rules, Regulations, Conditions and Methods
Guide for Grid Connection of Demand Installations to the Low Voltage Grid

latestUpdates: Verification note: this review does not establish the absence of important changes at the beginning of 2027. Current legislation, tariff decisions and operator requirements must be checked for the relevant connection.

Norway.title: Norway
gridConnectionProcedure: Norway applies grid connection codes for generators, demand connections and HVDC systems as part of Norwegian energy regulation. The Norwegian energy system is regulated by NVE/RME, with the Energy Act forming the main legal framework for electricity market regulation. Norway is not an EU Member State, but it is closely integrated into the Nordic and European electricity system through EEA-related regulation and Nordic market cooperation.
strategiesvolatility: Norway is highly relevant because of its very high EV penetration and strong reliance on electric heating.
Capacity-based grid tariffs for low-voltage customers were introduced to incentivise consumers to reduce peak loads and shift flexible consumption.

Voluntary conditional connection agreements can allow curtailment under agreed conditions and enable connections before reinforcement. They require agreement and are not an unconditional entitlement to network access.
regulatoryFramework: Norwegian Energy Act.
NVE/RME regulations on grid tariffs.
Norwegian implementation of grid connection codes: RfG, DCC and HVDC.
responsibleInstitutions: NVE: Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate.
RME: Norwegian Energy Regulatory Authority.
Statnett: transmission system operator.
Regional distribution system operators.
implementationExamples: Capacity-based network tariffs encourage households to avoid simultaneous high-power consumption.
Smart EV charging is used as a practical instrument to reduce local peak loads.
Non-firm connection agreements provide a regulatory tool for connecting flexible demand without immediately expanding the grid.
newconsumersandflexibleloads: Electric vehicles, electric heating, heat pumps, household batteries, distributed solar PV and flexible industrial demand.
EV charging is particularly important because unmanaged charging can create local peak-load problems, while smart charging can defer or reduce network reinforcement needs.

sources.name: Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate (NVE)

latestUpdates: Verification note: the reviewed material does not establish that no important changes will occur at the beginning of 2027. The relevant tariff and connection provisions require a project-specific update.

Sweden.title: Sweden
Sweden.gridConnectionProcedure: Generation developers should contact the relevant local or regional network operator to determine the appropriate connection level and technical requirements. Large projects may involve the transmission network. Differences between generation locations and demand centres create a need for network development and operational flexibility.
strategiesvolatility: Hydropower is an important source of dispatchable flexibility that can help balance variable wind and solar generation.
In addition, smart meters, dynamic electricity tariffs, demand response, local flexibility solutions, and smart grids are becoming increasingly important.
The regulator views smart grids as a tool for better integrating renewable energy, improving energy efficiency, and increasing grid reliability.
regulatoryFramework: The framework includes the Electricity Act (Ellag 1997:857), applicable EU electricity-market rules and national implementing provisions. New legislation, including Elmarknadslag 2026:1281, has been adopted for the subsequent framework; commencement and transitional provisions must be distinguished from the rules applicable on 28 October 2026.
Relevant aspects include grid connection requirements, network tariff regulation, requirements for smart metering systems, and rules governing the integration of flexibility.
Smart meters and demand-side flexibility are regarded not as isolated technologies but as integral components of a more efficient electricity market.
Network Tariff Regulation (2026): The Energy Markets Inspectorate repealed regulation EIFS 2022:1, removing the mandatory nationwide introduction of capacity-based network charges.
responsibleInstitutions: The Swedish Energy Markets Inspectorate (Ei) is the national energy regulator.
Svenska kraftnät is the transmission system operator.
Local and regional distribution system operators handle connections within their networks.
The Swedish Energy Agency (Energimyndigheten) administers energy programmes and supports research.
At the European level, ACER and ENTSO-E are also relevant.
implementationExamples: Sweden demonstrates how an electricity system with a high share of renewable generation can be stabilised through controllable hydropower and digital flexibility.
Smart meters, dynamic tariffs and demand response offer possible lessons for Germany, subject to differences in market rules and network conditions.
Germany can compare Swedish approaches to digitalisation and flexibility with its own framework. Section 14a EnWG is German law and must not be presented as a Swedish mechanism.
newconsumersandflexibleloads: In Sweden, new consumers are not only additional loads but also potential sources of flexibility.
Electric vehicles can shift charging times, heat pumps can be combined with thermal storage, and industrial processes can partially respond to electricity prices or grid conditions.
The Swedish Energy Markets Inspectorate (Ei) has identified demand-side flexibility as an important tool for an electricity system with a high share of variable generation.
For low-voltage grids, this means controllable consumers must increasingly become part of grid planning.

sources.name: IEA ISGAN: Metering as an Enabler for Consumer-Focused Flexibility in Sweden (2022; background)

latestUpdates: Ei repealed EIFS 2022:1 in June 2026, removing the planned obligation to introduce capacity-based tariffs by 1 January 2027. Compliant capacity charges remain possible.
EIFS 2026:8 introduces clearer customer-information requirements for electricity network operators from 1 January 2027.

Sweden has adopted new electricity legislation, including Elmarknadslag 2026:1281. The existing Ellag is scheduled for repeal on 1 January 2027; the new framework has its own commencement and transitional provisions.

Finland.title: Finland
gridConnectionProcedure: The expansion of wind power has significantly transformed Finland’s electricity system in recent years. Fingrid defines technical connection requirements through its Grid Code Specifications. These specify the technical and operational requirements that power plants must meet to reliably withstand voltage fluctuations, frequency deviations, and system disturbances. This is particularly important for renewable energy installations, as a high share of weather-dependent generation can only be integrated reliably if installations respond in a grid-supportive manner and exchange data with grid operators.
strategiesvolatility: Smart meters record consumption and generation at defined intervals. Data transmission, customer access and real-time control are separate capabilities and may have different delays.
Variable tariffs, demand response and balancing services can encourage flexibility where suitable controls and market arrangements are available.
regulatoryFramework: The legal framework includes the following legislation and technical requirements.
Finnish Electricity Market Act.
Applicable EU electricity-market legislation.
National grid connection rules.
Fingrid’s applicable technical connection requirements.
Requirements differ between generation, storage and demand connections.
Energiavirasto supervises the market and the network operators.

Fingrid specifies transmission-connection requirements. Separately, Section 65b of the Electricity Market Act requires DSOs to enable authorised market-based access to eligible meter load-control relays by 1 June 2027, subject to technical conditions.
On 12 June 2026, Fingrid introduced immediate supplementary technical requirements for relevant new or modified large demand facilities directly connected to the transmission grid, alongside KJV2018.
responsibleInstitutions: Energy and market regulatory authority (Energiavirasto).
Transmission system operator and system operator (Fingrid).
Finnish Energy and VTT provide industry expertise and research contributions.
ACER and ENTSO-E provide European reference frameworks for comparison.
implementationExamples: Digital metering supports billing, data exchange and flexibility services. Controlling a load also requires compatible equipment, communications, authorisation and, where relevant, market prequalification; a meter cannot operate every flexible load by itself.
newconsumersandflexibleloads: Electrification of heating, transport and industry creates additional electricity demand and potential flexibility.
Heat pumps can provide flexibility through thermal storage and controlled operation, subject to comfort and operating constraints.
Electric vehicles and industrial loads can be used as flexible consumers.
Qualifying demand-side resources can participate in reserve and balancing markets under the applicable technical and market requirements.
Fingrid reported approximately 1,050 MW of connected electricity storage in February 2026, including large systems and an estimate for small installations. MW measures power, not stored energy.

sources.name: National Report on electricity and gas markets in Finland in 2024 (Energiavirasto 2025)
VTT: Smart metering based demand response in Finland (research background)
Fingrid – Grid specifications for demand connections

latestUpdates: Fingrid has reported restrictions on new large battery connections in southern Finland until 2029 because of network constraints. This is a regional connection limitation, not a nationwide ban on storage.
KJV2026 remains a proposed demand-connection code at the review date. Fingrid targets regulatory confirmation in March 2027; the target date is not an already effective legal obligation.
Fingrid has announced a 4% increase in main grid service fees from 1 January 2027. This is not a 4% increase in every consumer’s total electricity bill.

United Kingdom.title: United Kingdom (Great Britain focus)
gridConnectionProcedure: In Great Britain, qualifying type-tested small generators with a rating up to and including 16 A per phase can use the G98 install-and-notify procedure, normally notifying the DNO within 28 days. G99 generally requires prior application for installations outside G98. Assessment times depend on the connection category; 45 days is not a universal deadline. Ofgem’s connection reforms have separate implementation and consultation stages.
strategiesvolatility: Market-wide Half-Hourly Settlement (MHHS) changes electricity-market settlement using half-hourly data. It does not require every household to receive half-hourly bills or take a dynamic tariff. Migration remains in progress at the review date.
regulatoryFramework: In Great Britain, the Smart Export Guarantee requires qualifying large suppliers to offer eligible small generators an export tariff under the scheme’s conditions.
SEG suppliers set their tariff rates, which must be greater than zero; there is no single government-set SEG rate.

Ofgem’s September 2026 connection review includes decisions and further consultations on transparency and customer service. The legal status and implementation date must be checked separately for each measure.

Proposed measures include demand-capacity registers, improved network-reinforcement information and consistent data standards. Consultation proposals are not binding merely because they have been published.
responsibleInstitutions: Ofgem regulates energy markets in Great Britain; Northern Ireland has a separate Utility Regulator.
NESO is Great Britain’s electricity system operator. Transmission network ownership and asset operation are undertaken by the relevant transmission owners.
Great Britain has 14 regional distribution licence areas, alongside independent distribution networks. Corporate ownership groups must be distinguished from licensed network areas.
implementationExamples: In Great Britain, covered private charge points must provide smart functionality and default settings avoiding charging from 08:00 to 11:00 and 16:00 to 22:00 on weekdays. Users can override the default schedule. The requirements apply to charge points within the regulations’ scope, not every private charger without exception.
newconsumersandflexibleloads: Great Britain has local flexibility procurement arrangements through which eligible resources can offer services to network operators.
DNOs regularly tender Flexibility Services, where aggregators bundle the capacity of private storage systems and heat pumps and use them for local grid stabilisation in exchange for remuneration.

latestUpdates: Ofgem’s 2026 connection review includes consultations closing on 6 November 2026 and further work planned for 2027. Final obligations and commencement dates depend on the relevant decisions and legal instruments.

Belgium.title: Belgium (Flanders)
Belgium.gridConnectionProcedure: For Flanders, generation equipment must meet applicable Synergrid technical requirements: C10/11 is the technical prescription, while C10/26 is the relevant homologation list. Fixed installations generally require AREI conformity inspection and notification to the network operator. Specific plug-and-play arrangements and existing metering must be considered separately.
strategiesvolatility: With digital meters in Flanders, electricity imports and exports are recorded separately. The replacement of legacy reversing meters and associated transitional arrangements mean that a blanket statement of complete abolition for every installation is too broad.

For relevant Flemish customers with digital meters, part of the network tariff is based on monthly maximum quarter-hour average import power, using the applicable averaging and billing rules. A minimum of 2.5 kW applies. Other tariff components remain energy-based, and different arrangements apply to analogue meters and protected categories.
regulatoryFramework: Belgium divides electricity responsibilities between federal and regional authorities. The Flemish network and tariff rules described here must not be applied automatically to Wallonia or Brussels.

Wallonia and Brussels have their own regulatory and tariff arrangements. The Flemish capacity tariff creates an incentive to manage import peaks but does not require a universal operating pattern for every household.
responsibleInstitutions: CREG is the federal electricity and gas regulator.
The Vlaamse Nutsregulator, formerly VREG, is the Flemish regulator.
CWaPE is the regional energy regulator for Wallonia.
BRUGEL is the regional energy regulator for the Brussels-Capital Region.
Fluvius operates distribution infrastructure on behalf of the relevant intermunicipal network entities in Flanders.
implementationExamples: A home energy management system can reduce coincident EV charging and other demand peaks. The 2.5 kW figure is a minimum billing basis, not a statutory household power limit or a guarantee that all loads can be kept below it.
newconsumersandflexibleloads: Home batteries can reduce import peaks when appropriately sized and controlled. Their economic value depends on tariffs, cycling, losses and investment costs; exceptionally high adoption caused by the capacity tariff has not been demonstrated here.

Brussels regulatory authority for electricity, gas and water price control

latestUpdates: Verification note: the review does not establish that no important Flemish electricity-rule or tariff changes will occur at the beginning of 2027.

Switzerland.title: Switzerland
Switzerland.gridConnectionProcedure: Applicants follow the responsible DSO’s connection procedure and applicable installation-safety rules, including a technical connection request and safety documentation where required. Metering and commissioning arrangements depend on the installation and network operator; a single mandatory sequence cannot be assumed for every project.
strategiesvolatility: Self-consumption communities (ZEV) and, under their respective conditions, virtual arrangements enable shared self-consumption. Local electricity communities (LEG), available from 2026, also allow eligible sharing through the public network; they differ from conventional behind-the-meter ZEV.

The smart-meter transition rule generally requires at least 80% coverage in each network area by the end of 2027, subject to the applicable provisions. This is not a requirement for universal 100% completion by that date.
regulatoryFramework: Self-consumption and export remuneration operate alongside the applicable renewable support schemes; surplus feed-in is not the only possible commercial arrangement.

In 2026, the statutory fallback remuneration uses the relevant quarterly reference market price when the producer and network operator have not agreed a price, subject to applicable minimum remuneration.

For qualifying PV installations, minimum remuneration is 6 Swiss centimes/kWh below 30 kW. From 30 kW to below 150 kW, it is 180/P centimes/kWh with self-consumption, where P is the installation capacity in kW, and 6.2 centimes/kWh without self-consumption.

From 1 January 2027, the revised statutory fallback remuneration is linked to the market price at the time of feed-in. Minimum-remuneration protection remains, with quarterly settlement of the relevant difference.
responsibleInstitutions: The Federal Electricity Commission (ElCom) is the national regulatory authority.
Swissgrid operates the transmission grid.
Switzerland has many distribution network operators of different sizes; they are not uniformly small or legally independent in the same sense.
implementationExamples: Some DSOs use ripple control or other load-management systems under the applicable technical and contractual arrangements.

Control or interruption of heat pumps and electric water heaters depends on the relevant DSO and contract. A nationwide rule requiring disconnection for up to two hours at midday has not been established.
newconsumersandflexibleloads: The relationship between import prices, export remuneration and equipment costs can encourage self-consumption, heat-pump scheduling and storage. Actual adoption and savings are site-specific.

sources.name: NA/EEA-NE7 – CH 2020 (historical technical guidance; check current DSO requirements)

latestUpdates: A material change is already scheduled for 1 January 2027: the revised statutory fallback export-remuneration method links remuneration to the market price at the time of feed-in while retaining minimum-remuneration protection.
